rationale: Both recall advance warning of suffering or persecution. Jesus' slave-and-master saying warns His followers about persecution; the letter says its prior prediction of affliction happened as the recipients know. The speakers, settings and fulfillment statement are not made identical.

The two prayers within the letter connect holiness and blamelessness with the Lord Jesus' coming. This prayer concerns hearts established blameless in holiness before God the Father at the Lord Jesus' coming with all His saints; the later one asks complete sanctification and preservation of spirit, soul and body. This is an internal prayer parallel, not independent testimony or a definition of every saint's identity.

Both direct readers away from sexual immorality. Thessalonians names abstaining within God's will for sanctification; Corinthians commands fleeing it and develops a body-related reason. The statement of God's will and the imperative retain their different forms and additional rationale.

Both internal prayers look to holiness and blamelessness at Jesus' coming. The earlier concerns hearts blameless in holiness before God the Father at the Lord Jesus' coming with all His saints; the closing prayer names the God of peace and whole spirit, soul and body. This does not independently settle a complete metaphysical account of human components.
